The `quayside` job queue in /app runs the background jobs of a shop back office: emails, refunds, invoice renders and stock moves. Since June 8 its dead-letter queue has kept growing. The queue logs are in /app/logs/queue; the worker, service, downstream, deploy, configuration and operator logs are in /app/logs; the state written at each stop is in /app/var/checkpoints; every revision of the configuration is in /app/config/history (the live file is /app/config/queue.toml); and /app/docs describes the queue. /app/docs/triage.md explains how dead letters are traced and lists the cause classes, and /app/tools/replay.py replays the logged traffic through a copy of the package.

Find every defect in the code shipped in /app/quayside that sends messages to the dead-letter queue that should not go there, and write /app/deadletter-report.json with one entry per defect:

    {"causes": [{"class": "<class>", "file": "<path>", "line": <number>, "messages": <count>, "first": "<message id>"}, ...]}

- `class`: one of the classes in /app/docs/triage.md section 3.
- `file` and `line`: the module, as a path relative to /app (for example `quayside/broker.py`), and the number of a line that is wrong, counted in the file as you received it, before your changes.
- `messages`: how many messages that the shipped release moved to the dead-letter queue, as logged in /app/logs/queue, would not have been dead-lettered by the end of the logs if only this defect had been fixed in the shipped code, with the same traffic, downstream answers, configuration reloads and restarts. A message can count for more than one defect, or for none, for example when it would take two fixes to keep it out.
- `first`: the id of the one of those messages whose `dead-letter` line comes first in /app/logs/queue, for example `m0004821`.

Messages dead-lettered by an earlier release are not counted. Only defects in the shipped code get an entry: traffic, payloads, configuration revisions, downstream services and restarts do not.

Then fix the code under /app/quayside so that the queue follows the docs. Do not change anything under /app/tests, /app/tools, /app/docs, /app/logs, /app/var or /app/config. The package will also be run on other traffic and configurations.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.

# Triage

How a dead-lettered message is traced to its cause.

## 1. Where to start

The `stats` lines in `logs/service.log` show, hour by hour, how many
messages went to the dead-letter queue. `logs/queue` has the reason the queue
gave for each one, and `logs/worker.log` every delivery before it. The
reason says what the queue decided, not why: a message can run out of
attempts because of an outage or because of a wrong count. A replay
(`operations.md` 5) runs the logged traffic through any copy of the package,
so the effect of one change to the code on every message can be measured:
run the copy and compare with the log.

## 2. Things that look wrong and are not

- A message whose handler failed `max_attempts` times while its downstream
  service was down for longer than the backoff covers.
- A refund to an expired card (`rejected`).
- A payload that really lacks a required field or has a schema version the
  configuration does not accept.
- A resend whose payload differs from the message holding its key, for
  example a support edit of an amount that was already refunded.
- A resend with the same payload (`duplicate`).
- Messages ended by an earlier release did what that release did. Check
  `logs/deploy.log`.
- A configuration revision that only moves or comments things.

## 3. Cause classes

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `retry-budget` | A message is given fewer (or more) failures than the docs allow before `attempts-exhausted` |
| `backoff` | The wait between deliveries after a failure is not the one the docs give |
| `idempotency` | Two messages get the same key when the docs give them different ones, or the reverse |
| `visibility` | A lease ends earlier or later than the docs give |
| `schema` | The payload check refuses a payload the docs accept, or the reverse |
| `routing` | A message reaches the wrong handler or downstream service |
| `ordering` | Things due at the same time happen in another order than the docs give |
| `clock` | Times are read, ordered or compared wrongly |

# Queue

All times are in milliseconds. A job type's settings (`max_attempts`,
`backoff`, `backoff_max`, `visibility`) are its own values from
`[jobs."<type>"]` in the configuration, or the global ones where it sets
none (`config.md` 3).

## 1. Messages and how they end

A producer enqueues a message with an id, a job type and a JSON payload
(`payloads.md`). The message is ready at once. Every message ends exactly
once:

- `done`: a delivery's handler returned `ok`.
- `duplicate`: the message repeats one that holds its idempotency key
  (section 5). Its handler does not run.
- `dead-letter`: the message is moved to the dead-letter queue with one of
  the reasons in section 6.

## 2. Deliveries

Workers deliver every ready message at once; there is no limit on how many
deliveries run at the same time. A delivery:

1. counts one more receive of the message;
2. checks the payload (`payloads.md`); a payload that fails the check goes to
   the dead-letter queue with reason `schema-rejected`, on any receive;
3. on the message's first delivery that passes the payload check, checks its
   idempotency key (section 5);
4. takes a lease (section 4) and runs the handler.

When several things are due at the same millisecond, results come first,
then lease expiries, then deliveries.

## 3. Results

The handler returns one of four results:

- `ok`: the message is `done`.
- `rejected`: the downstream service refused the message for good (for
  example an expired card). The message goes to the dead-letter queue with
  reason `rejected`; it is not retried.
- `throttled`: the downstream service asked for fewer calls and said when to
  come back (`retry_after`). The message is ready again `retry_after` after
  the result. A throttled delivery is not a failure: it does not count
  toward `max_attempts`, however many times it happens.
- `error`: the downstream service failed (a timeout, a 5xx). This is a
  failure. When the message has failed `max_attempts` times it goes to the
  dead-letter queue with reason `attempts-exhausted`. Otherwise it is ready
  again after the backoff for its failure count `n`:
  `backoff * 2^(n-1)`, never more than `backoff_max`. With `backoff = "1m"`
  and `backoff_max = "15m"` the waits are 1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 15, ... minutes.

## 4. Leases

A delivery holds the message for `visibility`, its job type's visibility
timeout, from the time it starts. While the handler runs, and
`lease.heartbeat` is true, the worker renews the lease every third of the
job type's visibility timeout (integer division of the milliseconds): each
renewal moves the end of the lease to `visibility` after the renewal. A
renewal is only possible while the lease still holds, so with heartbeats on
a lease does not run out while its worker is up. With `heartbeat = false`
nothing renews it.

If the lease runs out before the handler returns, the message is ready again
at that moment and is delivered again; the result of the old delivery, when
it comes, is refused and changes nothing. A lease that runs out at the same
millisecond as the handler returns does not run out: the result counts. Each
lease that runs out counts as a lost lease; when a message has lost
`lease.max_lost` leases it goes to the dead-letter queue with reason
`lease-lost`.

When the queue stops (`operations.md` 2), running deliveries are abandoned
without a result. Their message is ready again when its lease, as it stood at
the stop, ends; an abandoned delivery is not a lost lease.

## 5. Idempotency keys

A producer that is not sure a message went through sends it again with the
same payload. The key of a message is:

- `<type>:<idem>` when the payload is schema 3 or later and has a non-empty
  `idem` field;
- `<type>:<idem_key>` when the payload is schema 2 and has a non-empty
  `idem_key` field;
- `<type>:order:<order>` otherwise.

A schema 3 payload's `idem_key` and a schema 2 payload's `idem` play no part
in the key.

The first message to pass the key check with a free key holds it. Another
message with the same key is a `duplicate` when its payload equals the
holder's, every field but `sent_at` compared, and goes to the dead-letter
queue with reason `key-conflict` when it differs. A message never conflicts
with itself: later deliveries of the holder skip the check. The holder keeps
the key while it is pending and for `dedupe.window` after it is `done`; a
holder that goes to the dead-letter queue frees the key at once, so a fixed
message can be sent again.

## 6. Dead-letter reasons

| Reason | When |
|---|---|
| `schema-rejected` | the payload check failed (section 2) |
| `key-conflict` | the key is held by a message with another payload (section 5) |
| `rejected` | the handler returned `rejected` (section 3) |
| `attempts-exhausted` | the message failed `max_attempts` times (section 3) |
| `lease-lost` | the message lost `lease.max_lost` leases (section 4) |
# Configuration

The live file is `config/queue.toml`. Every revision ever applied is kept in
`config/history/r<rev>.toml` (three digits), and `logs/config.log` says when
each was applied. A reload takes effect for deliveries that start after it;
running deliveries keep the lease they started with.

## 1. Example

```toml
rev = 7
accept_schema = [2, 3]

[retry]
max_attempts = 6
backoff = "1m"
backoff_max = "15m"

[lease]
visibility = "10m"
heartbeat = true
max_lost = 4

[dedupe]
window = "24h"

[jobs."refund.issue"]
max_attempts = 10
backoff = "2m"
```

## 2. Keys

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rev` | the revision number |
| `accept_schema` | the payload schema versions the queue accepts (`payloads.md` 1) |
| `retry.max_attempts` | failures before `attempts-exhausted` (`queue.md` 3) |
| `retry.backoff`, `retry.backoff_max` | the first wait after a failure and the longest (`queue.md` 3) |
| `lease.visibility` | the visibility timeout (`queue.md` 4); at least 3 seconds |
| `lease.heartbeat` | whether running deliveries renew their lease (`queue.md` 4) |
| `lease.max_lost` | lost leases before `lease-lost` (`queue.md` 4) |
| `dedupe.window` | how long a `done` message keeps its key (`queue.md` 5) |

A duration is a whole number of seconds (`90`), or a string with one unit:
`ms`, `s`, `m` or `h` (`"90s"`, `"2m"`).

## 3. Job types

A `[jobs."<type>"]` table may set `max_attempts`, `backoff`, `backoff_max`
and `visibility` for one job type. Everything it does not set comes from the
global tables. `heartbeat`, `max_lost`, `accept_schema` and the dedupe window
are global only.

Long handlers such as invoice renders do not need a long visibility timeout:
with heartbeats on, the lease is renewed for as long as the handler runs, and
a short timeout brings back the messages of a worker that died sooner.
# Payloads

A payload is a JSON object. Every payload has a whole-number schema version
`v` and the time the producer sent it, `sent_at`.

## 1. The check before a handler runs

A payload passes when:

- `v` is a whole number listed in `accept_schema` (`config.md` 2), and
- every required field of its job type is present:

| Job type | Required fields |
|---|---|
| `email.send` | `order`, `to`, `template` |
| `refund.issue` | `order`, `amount`, `card` |
| `invoice.render` | `order`, `lines` |
| `stock.sync` | `order`, `sku`, `qty` |

Fields a job type does not list are ignored, in every schema version, so
that producers can add fields before every handler reads them. A payload is
never refused for carrying them.

## 2. Idempotency fields

- Schema 3 names the producer's idempotency value `idem`.
- Schema 2 named it `idem_key`.

Producers moving from schema 2 to 3 sometimes keep sending the old field
next to the new one; only the field of the payload's own version counts
(`queue.md` 5).

## 3. Producers

| Producer | Job types | Schema |
|---|---|---|
| `notifier` | `email.send` | 2 |
| `campaigns` | `email.send` (newsletters, `order` is `-`) | 2 |
| `billing` | `refund.issue` | 3 |
| `support` | `refund.issue` (resends after a manual edit) | 3 |
| `pos` | `refund.issue` (store terminals) | 3 |
| `storefront` | `invoice.render`, `stock.sync` | 3 |
# Operations

## 1. Logs

All times are UTC.

- `logs/queue/<date>.log`: the queue's own record, in order. One `enqueue`
  line per message, with its id, job type, producer and payload:

  ```
  2027-06-08T14:02:11.204Z enqueue m0004821 refund.issue producer=billing {"amount":1250,"card":"ok","idem":"rf-o101377-1","order":"o101377","sent_at":"2027-06-08T14:02:11.010Z","v":3}
  ```

  and one line when the message ends (`queue.md` 1): `done <id>`,
  `duplicate <id> of=<holder id>`, or `dead-letter <id> reason=<reason>`.
- `logs/worker.log`: every delivery that got as far as a result, a refusal,
  a lost lease or an abandonment: `<id> receive=<n>` followed by
  `ok ms=<ms>`, `error ms=<ms> "<detail>"`,
  `throttled ms=<ms> retry_after=<ms>ms "<detail>"`,
  `rejected ms=<ms> "<detail>"` (a result line, written when the handler
  returns, with `ack refused (lease lost)` when it came too late),
  `refused "<why>"` (the payload or key check), `lease expired` or
  `abandoned`.
- `logs/service.log`: `started config=r<rev>` (with the checkpoint it read),
  `stopping checkpoint=<file>`, `config reload rev=<rev>`, and once an hour a
  `stats` line for the hour before it: messages enqueued, ended `done`,
  `duplicate` and `dead_lettered` in the hour, the messages pending at the
  end of the hour (`backlog`) and the dead-letter queue's size (`dlq`).
- `logs/downstream.log`: every change of state of a downstream service, as
  the services report it: `ok`, `down`, or `throttled` with the
  `retry_after` it sends back.
- `logs/deploy.log`: releases, with the time each went live, and other
  teams' releases that change what producers send.
- `logs/config.log`: configuration revisions, with the time each was applied.
- `logs/ops.log`: notes by the operators.

## 2. Restarts and deploys

The queue stops before a deploy or a host change and starts again a few
seconds later. Producers hold their messages while it is stopped. A release
runs from the first `started` line after its deploy time until the next
deploy; the `drain` lines in the deploy log mark the deploy window, and the
queue keeps delivering until `stopping`. A host restart without a deploy (for
example a kernel patch) starts the release that was already running.

## 3. Checkpoints

At `stopping` the queue writes its state to `var/checkpoints/<time>.json`
and the next `started` line reads it: every pending message (payload,
receives, failures, lost leases, when it is ready, whether it holds its key)
and every held idempotency key. Nothing else carries over a restart.

## 4. Applying a configuration

`config reload` applies a revision without a restart (`config.md`).

## 5. Replaying traffic

```
python3 tools/replay.py [--since TIME] [--until TIME] [--diff] [--times] [--pkg DIR] [--root DIR]
```

reads the logs, the configuration history and the checkpoints, and runs
every message, reload, stop and start through the package in log order,
starting at the last `started` line at or before `--since` (the first one
without it) with the checkpoint that line read. Each handler call gets the
answer its downstream service gave at that moment according to
`downstream.log`, and takes as long as the same call took in the logs.

It prints one line per message that ended at or after `--since` (or is still
pending) with how the log and the replay ended it, for example

```
m0004821 logged=dead-letter:key-conflict@2027-06-08T18:02:14.411Z replay=done
```

and a summary line. `--diff` prints only the messages where the two differ;
`--times` adds when the replay ended each message and after how many
receives. Times are written as in the logs, for example
`2027-06-08T14:00:05.000Z`. `--pkg` names a directory that holds a
`quayside` package to use instead of `/app/quayside`, for example a copy
with one change, and `--root` a directory laid out like `/app` with other
logs. Every `started` line runs the same package, so a replay reproduces the
log only over the time the release in `--pkg` actually ran.

# Overview

`quayside` is the job queue of the shop back office. Producers enqueue
messages; workers deliver each message to the handler of its job type, and
the handler calls one downstream service:

| Job type | Producer | Downstream service | What the handler does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `email.send` | `notifier`, `campaigns` | `mailer` | sends one email |
| `refund.issue` | `billing`, `support`, `pos` | `payments` | issues one refund to a card |
| `invoice.render` | `storefront` | `pdfgen` | renders the invoice PDF of an order, one page section per line |
| `stock.sync` | `storefront` | `inventory` | moves stock for an order |

A message ends in one of three ways (`queue.md` 1): its handler succeeds
(`done`), it repeats a message that already holds its idempotency key
(`duplicate`), or it goes to the dead-letter queue (`dead-letter`, with a
reason). Messages in the dead-letter queue stay there until an operator
looks at them; nothing in the queue retries them.

## Layout

- `quayside/`: the package. `broker.py` runs deliveries, leases and results;
  `retry.py` decides what a result does to a message; `lease.py` computes
  leases and heartbeats; `dedupe.py` builds and holds idempotency keys;
  `schema.py` checks payloads; `config.py` reads the configuration;
  `checkpoint.py` writes and reads the state kept across restarts.
- `config/queue.toml`: the live configuration. `config/history/` keeps every
  revision (`config.md`).
- `logs/`, `var/checkpoints/`: what the queue did (`operations.md`).
- `tools/replay.py`: replays the logged traffic through a copy of the
  package (`operations.md` 5).
- `tests/`: unit tests, run with `python3 -m unittest` from this directory.
